Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The QR factorization of an [MATH: m\times n] matrix [MATH: A] with linearly independent columns is the matrix product
[MATH: \underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is an [MATH: m \times n] matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] and
- [MATH: R] is an [MATH: n \times n] upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its diagonal.

Content:
For example, the [MATH: 3\times 2] matrix

Content:
[MATH: [2|− 3; − 4|3; 4|0]]

Content:
has the QR factorization

Content:
[MATH: [2|− 3; − 4|3; 4|0]]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: A=QR] is a QR factorization of an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] then

[MATH: \underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},]

where

- [MATH: Q] is an [MATH: m \times n] matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of [MATH: \text{Col}(A)]
- [MATH: R] is an [MATH: n \times n] upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. [MATH: Q] should be a [MATH: 3\times 2] matrix.
- Statement II is true. Indeed, the columns of [MATH: Q] form an orthonormal basis of [MATH: \text{Col}(A).]
- Statement III is true. Indeed, [MATH: R] must be a [MATH: 2 \times 2] upper triangular matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
